newsitem.title: POLAND: World Bank chief expects to back Romania reforms.
newsitem.headline: World Bank chief expects to back Romania reforms.

text.p: World Bank President James Wolfensohn said on Friday he would restate full support for Romania's reform plans if he found, during a visit there next week, that the country was indeed doing what it had promised.

Wolfensohn, due to leave for Romania on Sunday after a five-day official visit in Poland, said he had already met President Emil Constantinescu, who ousted an ex-communist in last year's election, and the country's finance minister.
"I have assured them of significant World Bank support in the conduct of their announced plans for the reform of the Romanian economy," he told a news conference in Warsaw.
"My purpose in visiting is to understand and, if I am convinced that they are doing what I think they are doing, I will reassert the full support of the bank," he said.
He said he had no doubt Romania would be very pleased with the terms of World Bank lending.
The Bank said on Thursday it had agreed to extend credits worth about $300 million to Romania ahead of the visit.

The credits are subject to approval at a meeting next month of the Bank's board, along with a further credit under discussion, bringing to about $500 million the total structural assistance the Balkan country can expect to receive.

The World Bank's chief of mission in Bucharest, Francois Ettori, said Wolfensohn's visit reflected approval in the West of the new centrist government's pledges to proceed quickly with market reforms after seven years of slow progress.
But he said committed reformers at the top had to struggle with a bureaucratic machine.
Both the IMF and World Bank stopped lending programmes last year, saying the leftist government of the time had fallen short on reform promises and overspent ahead of the election.

But the freeing of prices, adoption of an austerity budget and pledges to shut down loss-making state firms persuaded the International Monetary Fund last month to approve $430 million in credits for Romania.
